paragraphs: When an analyst needs average values for several groups, a limited sampling budget raises a practical question: which group should be measured next? This paper studies a sequential setting where each observation comes from one chosen group. The groups’ distributions are unknown, so the analyst must learn their means and variances while deciding how to allocate observations.

The proposed Variance-UCB algorithm selects groups using upper bounds on their estimated variances. Its choices also depend on a parameter, p, that determines how the uncertainties across groups are combined into one objective. For finite p, the objective aggregates those uncertainties; at infinite p, it focuses on the largest one. Sampling decisions therefore respond both to observed variability and to the chosen evaluation criterion.

The authors prove regret rates of O(T^-2) for finite p and O(T^-1.5) for infinite p, where T is the sampling budget. Matching lower bounds establish that these rates cannot be improved in the studied setting. These are guarantees about regret in sample allocation, rather than claims that every mean estimate has error decreasing at those rates.
neurips-2023-an-active-learning-framewor.tldr: Variance-UCB adaptively allocates observations across groups and achieves optimal regret rates for the studied mean-estimation objectives.

paragraphs: Some tasks are easy for people to recognize as successful but difficult to specify precisely for an algorithm. The BASALT Minecraft tasks explore this problem through activities such as creating and photographing a waterfall. BEDD turns material from two years of these competitions into a formal benchmark for developing and assessing agents that tackle such loosely specified goals.

The dataset contains 26 million image-action pairs drawn from nearly 14,000 videos of human players completing the tasks. These demonstrations record both what players saw and what they did. A separate evaluation collection supplies more than 3,000 dense pairwise human judgments comparing human and algorithmic agents, providing evidence about how people assess task performance.

The comparisons form a fixed, preliminary leaderboard, and an accompanying codebase supports benchmarking new algorithms against it. The paper also analyzes both collections to help researchers use them for training and evaluation. Its contribution is a shared resource connecting demonstrations with human assessments, making progress on tasks with difficult-to-formalize success criteria easier to compare.
neurips-2023-bedd-the-minerl-basalt-eval.tldr: BEDD combines Minecraft demonstrations and human comparisons into a benchmark for agents solving hard-to-specify tasks.

paragraphs: A hypergraph represents interactions involving groups of participants, rather than only pairs. A temporal hypergraph also records how those interactions unfold over time. CAT-Walk learns representations for this setting, aiming to capture the structural and temporal patterns governing group interactions. This addresses a gap left by methods designed mainly for static hypergraphs or individual tasks.

Its central component, SetWalk, follows temporal, higher-order walks to extract interaction patterns. SetMixer then combines the resulting information through adaptive pooling that does not depend on the ordering of set elements. A set-based anonymization procedure hides hyperedge identities, and a neural network encodes the hyperedges. Together, these components support learning interaction patterns without relying on a fixed ordering or specific hyperedge names.

Across 10 benchmark datasets, the authors report strong temporal hyperedge prediction results in both inductive and transductive settings. They also report competitive node-classification performance against state-of-the-art methods. The findings support using the learned representations for more than one prediction task, with particular strength in predicting time-dependent group interactions.
neurips-2023-cat-walk-inductive-hypergra.tldr: CAT-Walk learns temporal hypergraph representations through set-based walks, identity hiding, and order-invariant pooling.

paragraphs: Observed data can mix together hidden factors that influence one another. Independent Component Analysis seeks independent factors, while causal representation learning also tries to discover their causal relationships. This paper introduces Causal Component Analysis, an intermediate problem that assumes the causal graph is already known and learns how to separate the observations and recover the causal mechanisms.

The authors characterize when those hidden components can be identified using multiple datasets produced by interventions on the latent variables. The known-graph assumption makes the problem more focused: impossibility results also constrain the broader causal representation learning problem, while successful recovery results may help develop solutions for it. An empty causal graph gives nonlinear ICA as a special case.

This intervention-based analysis yields new nonlinear ICA identifiability results requiring strictly fewer datasets than previous results. The paper also develops a likelihood-based estimator using normalizing flows to learn both the unmixing function and causal mechanisms. Synthetic experiments demonstrate its effectiveness in the CauCA and ICA settings, connecting the recovery analysis to a practical estimation approach.
neurips-2023-causal-component-analysis-7.tldr: Causal Component Analysis studies recovering interacting hidden factors when their causal graph is known, with intervention-based guarantees and a flow-based estimator.

paragraphs: Anchor acceleration is a mechanism for speeding up algorithms for minimax optimization and fixed-point problems. Although it has achieved accelerated convergence, the reasons for its effectiveness have been less well understood than those of Nesterov acceleration. This paper studies the mechanism by analyzing continuous-time models, which describe the evolution of the optimization process through time.

The analysis centers on the anchor coefficient, beta(t), and how its behavior determines convergence speed. The authors provide tight, unified characterizations of the convergence rate as a function of that coefficient. This connects a controllable part of the method to its mathematical performance and gives insight into the accelerated O(1/k^2) rate associated with anchor acceleration.

The paper then uses these continuous-time insights to develop an adaptive method, moving from explanation toward algorithm design. Its effectiveness is supported by both theoretical analysis and experiments. The contribution is therefore twofold: a more systematic account of how the anchor coefficient affects acceleration, and an adaptive approach motivated by that account.
neurips-2023-continuous-time-analysis-of.tldr: Continuous-time analysis explains how the anchor coefficient controls acceleration and motivates an adaptive optimization method.

paragraphs: Language models can learn tasks from very few examples, but that limited-data setting also creates challenges for detecting backdoor attacks. The paper begins with a pilot study finding that pretrained language models used as few-shot learners are highly vulnerable and that existing defenses are inadequate for the particular demands of this setting.

The proposed defense, MDP, examines how a sample’s internal representation changes when different parts of it are masked. It uses the small set of available few-shot examples as reference points for the data distribution. Samples whose representations vary substantially under masking are identified as poisoned, exploiting a difference in masking sensitivity between clean and poisoned inputs.

The authors analytically show that this detection strategy creates a trade-off for attackers between maintaining attack effectiveness and avoiding detection. Evaluations with benchmark datasets and representative attacks support the defense’s effectiveness. MDP is presented as lightweight and pluggable, making the main contribution a detection mechanism suited to scarce reference data rather than a requirement to build a separate defense around abundant examples.
neurips-2023-defending-pre-trained-langu.tldr: MDP detects backdoor-poisoned inputs in few-shot language learning by measuring representation changes under masking.

paragraphs: This paper explores diffusion models as a way to learn graph representations without supervision. Its starting point is that graphs can contain anisotropic structure: meaningful variation is not distributed equally across all directions. Standard forward diffusion adds isotropic Gaussian noise, which treats directions uniformly and may wash out these unevenly distributed signals too quickly.

When meaningful structure becomes noise rapidly, the reverse denoising process becomes harder to learn and may produce less useful representations. The proposed directional diffusion models change the forward process itself. They introduce noise that depends on the data and varies by direction, adapting the corruption process to the structure the representation learner needs to capture.

The authors evaluate the models on 12 public datasets across two graph representation learning tasks and report better performance than state-of-the-art baselines. These findings support their argument that the choice of forward noise matters for learning meaningful graph features. The work identifies direction-sensitive corruption as a useful design choice for the evaluated graph-learning settings.
neurips-2023-directional-diffusion-model.tldr: Directional diffusion adapts noise to graph structure to improve unsupervised representation learning.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a student model using guidance from a teacher. This paper investigates whether pretrained foundation models can teach vision models to remain reliable when the data differ from the training distribution. The authors report strong robustness gains, providing evidence against the conjecture that larger models do not make better teachers.

Their method, Discrete Adversarial Distillation, combines teacher guidance with a particular form of data augmentation. A robust teacher generates adversarial examples, and a VQGAN discretizes those examples. The resulting samples are intended to be more informative for student training than standard augmentations, bringing the teacher’s robustness into the construction of the training data as well as the distillation process.

The paper supplies a theoretical framework for using robust teachers in distillation with augmentation. Experiments show gains in both out-of-distribution robustness and clean accuracy across different student architectures. The method adds only minor computational overhead compared with similar techniques and can be combined with other augmentations, supporting its use as a lightweight addition to student training.
neurips-2023-distilling-out-of-distribut.tldr: Discrete Adversarial Distillation uses robust foundation-model teachers and discretized adversarial examples to improve student accuracy and distribution-shift robustness.

paragraphs: Images designed to strongly activate neurons can help reveal what a visual system responds to. This paper first improves the predictive model used for that purpose: an attention-inspired readout paired with a data-driven convolutional core predicts macaque V4 activity better than previous task-driven models. More complex predictors, however, can make image optimization vulnerable to model-specific quirks.

The authors introduce Energy Guidance for diffusion, or EGG, to generate neurally exciting images. Straightforward gradient ascent can overfit a predictor’s idiosyncrasies, potentially weakening transfer to the brain. For macaque V4 models, EGG produces single-neuron stimuli that generalize better across model architectures than gradient ascent while reducing computational costs by a factor of 4.7.

EGG also generates naturalistic exciting images with performance comparable to selected highly activating natural images, and reconstructions that transfer better across architectures. It requires no retraining of the diffusion model. These results support a flexible framework for probing visual coding, with lower computational costs potentially helping demanding closed-loop experiments; the reported cross-architecture gains are specifically evidence about transfer between models.
neurips-2023-energy-guided-diffusion-for.tldr: EGG guides diffusion to generate neurally exciting images that transfer better across V4 model architectures at lower computational cost.

paragraphs: Multimodal contrastive learning uses paired observations, such as images and captions, to learn from unlabeled data. A common assumption is that information shared across the modalities is enough for downstream tasks. This paper challenges that assumption because useful information may appear in just one modality and therefore be overlooked by a method focused on agreement.

FactorCL explicitly separates representations for shared information and information unique to each modality. Its objectives use bounds on mutual information, a measure of statistical dependence: maximizing lower bounds helps retain task-relevant content, while minimizing upper bounds helps remove irrelevant content. Multimodal augmentations approximate which information matters for the task without requiring labels.

On large-scale real-world datasets, the authors find that FactorCL captures both shared and unique information and achieves state-of-the-art results on six benchmarks. The contribution is a way to learn from paired modalities without treating their overlap as the whole useful signal. Its factorization makes room for complementary evidence that a shared-only representation could discard.
neurips-2023-factorized-contrastive-lear.tldr: FactorCL learns both shared and modality-specific information, improving multimodal representations beyond an agreement-only approach.

paragraphs: Choosing among pretrained models can be expensive if every candidate must be fine-tuned on every target dataset. This paper asks whether their suitability can instead be estimated across varied multimodal tasks, including recognition, captioning, referring, and question answering. Existing lightweight transferability measures often depend on task-specific knowledge, making that broader comparison difficult.

EMMS uses foundation models to convert different label formats, including categories, text, and bounding boxes, into a common noisy embedding representation. It then estimates a candidate model’s transferability with weighted linear regression. An alternating minimization algorithm solves this regression efficiently, with a convergence guarantee. The shared representation lets one selection framework work across otherwise incompatible label formats.

Experiments cover five downstream tasks and 24 datasets. Against LogME augmented with the same label embeddings, EMMS reports performance gains ranging from 9.0% to 54.8% across the tasks, alongside wall-clock speedups from 3.59 to 6.29 times. These results concern the model-selection procedure, supporting faster assessment of candidate models without fine-tuning every candidate on each target dataset.
neurips-2023-foundation-model-is-efficie.tldr: EMMS uses foundation-model label embeddings and weighted regression to efficiently estimate pretrained models’ transferability across multimodal tasks.

paragraphs: Understanding a scene requires grouping sensory information into distinct entities and recognizing familiar components in new combinations. This paper studies that ability through GUST, an iterative spiking network inspired by evidence linking successful grouping in the brain to neuronal coherence. The aim is to make grouping emerge in the timing of neural activity.

Biological constraints bias the network toward coherent activity patterns that softly encode which information belongs together. Rather than relying on explicit grouping labels, GUST learns to separate superimposed stimuli through a concise unsupervised objective. Grouping is therefore expressed through the network’s evolving temporal behavior, with spike timing carrying information about the structure of the input.

Evaluations on synthetic datasets reveal two learning stages: the model first captures coarse global features and then additionally learns local features. The resulting symbol-like components can be composed systematically to represent novel scenes. These findings connect unsupervised segregation with combinatorial generalization in the studied synthetic setting, showing how reusable building blocks can arise within a biologically constrained architecture.
neurips-2023-gust-combinatorial-generali.tldr: GUST learns to group superimposed stimuli through coherent spike timing and recombines learned components to represent novel synthetic scenes.

paragraphs: Transferable adversarial examples are altered inputs that can fool models beyond the one used to construct them. Intermediate-level attacks pursue this by changing internal feature representations. Existing approaches often first choose an adversarial direction and then increase the feature perturbation’s projection onto that direction, treating guidance and perturbation growth as separate stages.

The paper identifies a weakness in that separation: the actual feature change inevitably deviates from the guide, and this deviation may produce a suboptimal attack. Intermediate-level Perturbation Decay, or ILPD, instead uses one optimization stage. It simultaneously encourages the perturbation to point in an effective adversarial direction and to have a large magnitude, addressing direction and strength together.

Experiments across various victim models report average improvements of 10.07% on ImageNet and 3.88% on CIFAR-10 over state-of-the-art approaches. These findings support the proposed joint treatment of direction and magnitude for improving attack transferability. The explanation concerns the behavior of intermediate feature perturbations, connecting a geometric weakness in prior methods to the observed empirical gains.
neurips-2023-improving-adversarial-trans.tldr: ILPD jointly optimizes the direction and magnitude of intermediate feature perturbations to improve adversarial transferability.

paragraphs: Latent graph inference learns both a graph’s connections and representations of its nodes from data features. With few labeled examples, many learned edge weights receive no semantic supervision through the training loss. The paper calls this supervision starvation and links it to poor generalization because those insufficiently supervised connections still influence predictions on test samples.

The authors identify graph sparsification as the source of the problem: removing connections can sever important paths between pivotal nodes and labeled nodes. They define the affected nodes as k-hop starved nodes, identify them from the adjacency matrix, and reconstruct lost affinities to restore supervision. A more efficient alternative inspired by CUR matrix decomposition reduces the computational burden of identifying critical nodes.

Experiments show that reducing the number of starved nodes consistently improves state-of-the-art latent graph inference methods on representative benchmarks. Gains are especially pronounced with extremely limited supervision, including a reported 6.12% improvement on Pubmed at a 0.3% labeling rate. The results emphasize that retaining useful routes to labels matters alongside learning the graph itself.
neurips-2023-latent-graph-inference-with.tldr: Restoring graph connections lost during sparsification improves latent graph inference by reconnecting supervision-starved nodes to labeled information.

paragraphs: Neural implicit reconstruction learns a continuous representation of a scene from multiple images. Volume rendering connects that representation to observed color or depth views. The paper identifies a weakness in supervising one view at a time: holes in a depth image and structures hidden from that viewpoint leave incomplete guidance for learning the scene’s geometry.

The proposed approach combines all available depth images into a Truncated Signed Distance Function, or TSDF, which supplies a coarse account of the scene’s three-dimensional structure. An attention mechanism lets the network use this fused depth prior while learning an occupancy-based implicit representation. Information visible in other depth views can consequently inform regions missing or occluded in the current view.

The mechanism works with either a TSDF fused once for a whole scene or an incrementally updated TSDF representing a partial scene during simultaneous localization and mapping. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world scan benchmarks outperform the compared recent neural implicit methods. The contribution is to integrate cross-view depth knowledge directly into geometry learning through rendering.
neurips-2023-learning-neural-implicit-th.tldr: An attention-based fused-depth prior improves neural implicit reconstruction by bringing cross-view geometry into volume-rendering supervision.

paragraphs: Clustering pipelines often reduce dimensionality before assigning data points to groups. Spectral tools such as PCA and singular value decomposition frequently improve the resulting clusters, suggesting that they do more than compress the data. This paper investigates that additional contribution by studying a basic SVD algorithm in the stochastic block model, a mathematical setting for graph clustering.

The central result is exact recovery of all clusters by vanilla SVD in the symmetric setting studied by the authors. Recovering every cluster correctly is a stronger conclusion than merely obtaining a useful low-dimensional representation or improving an average clustering score. It directly connects the spectral step to the underlying group structure in this setting.

The result resolves a previously posed open question for the symmetric case. Its significance is theoretical: it gives a concrete account of the clustering power of a familiar dimensionality-reduction tool. The symmetric stochastic block model is the stated scope of the conclusion, so the result should be understood within that setting rather than extended to arbitrary clustering problems.
neurips-2023-on-the-power-of-svd-in-the-.tldr: The paper proves that vanilla SVD correctly recovers all clusters in the studied symmetric stochastic block model.

paragraphs: A deterministic partial differential equation can still be solved using uncertain data. This paper asks how confidence intervals at observed data locations can be carried through the equation to describe uncertainty throughout the domain. The goal is to propagate confidence with probabilistic guarantees, extending information available at particular locations to the wider solution.

The authors introduce Physics-Informed Confidence Propagation, or PICProp, using bilevel optimization to compute a valid confidence interval. Their motivation is that standard uncertainty-quantification approaches can depend heavily on likelihood assumptions and prior choices, while approximate posterior sampling can become computationally costly. PICProp approaches the problem through confidence-interval estimation without requiring heavy assumptions.

The paper provides a theorem establishing the validity of the method and computational experiments focused on physics-informed learning. Its contribution is both a formulation of confidence propagation for deterministic equations and an optimization-based method for carrying it out. The resulting intervals aim to retain a probabilistic interpretation as uncertainty moves from the data locations across the equation’s domain.
neurips-2023-picprop-physics-informed-co.tldr: PICProp uses bilevel optimization to propagate confidence intervals from observed data across deterministic PDE domains with validity guarantees.

paragraphs: Generative image models face a trade-off between producing convincing individual images and covering a broad range of possibilities. The paper describes these goals as precision and recall. Although principled ways to evaluate them exist, training has largely relied on heuristic objectives. The authors propose training GANs and normalizing flows directly for a user-selected precision-recall balance.

The mathematical contribution connects each specified trade-off to minimizing a unique member of a family called PR-divergences. A divergence measures a difference between probability distributions, so this connection turns the desired balance into a training objective. Conversely, the authors show that any f-divergence can be expressed as a linear combination of PR-divergences, corresponding to a weighted precision-recall trade-off.

Evaluations show improvements in either precision or recall for existing models, including BigGAN on datasets such as ImageNet. The finding supports explicit control over which aspect of generation is emphasized. It does not imply that every choice improves both goals simultaneously; the method is designed to optimize the balance selected by the user.
neurips-2023-precision-recall-divergence.tldr: PR-divergences turn a user-chosen balance between image quality and diversity into an explicit generative-model training objective.

paragraphs: Segmenting multiple objects in real videos is difficult without annotations. Additional cues such as motion or depth can help on synthetic sequences, but the paper notes that those gains do not necessarily carry over to challenging real footage. The authors propose a fully unsupervised approach that builds object representations from semantic features and their relationships over time.

The framework assigns spatial information within each frame to object slots, then connects those slots across frames. These temporally informed representations are trained to reconstruct the middle frame in a high-level semantic feature space. The objective therefore uses information across time while organizing the scene into separate object-centered representations.

A masking strategy drops a substantial fraction of feature tokens to improve efficiency and provide regularization. The method also merges similar slots to address over-clustering, where too many groups represent the scene. The authors demonstrate segmentation of multiple instances from complex and varied classes in YouTube videos, supporting the approach’s usefulness on real-world sequences rather than only synthetic scenes.
neurips-2023-self-supervised-object-cent.tldr: The method learns object slots across video frames and reconstructs semantic features to segment real-world videos without supervision.

paragraphs: Semantic image synthesis turns a user’s region labels into a realistic image with the requested spatial arrangement. Conventional approaches require expensive pixel-level training annotations. Pretrained unconditional generators already contain useful visual structure, but directly manipulating their intermediate features typically offers only coarse control. This paper develops a way to apply detailed user masks to such generators.

A semantic mapper translates the user’s guiding mask into a proxy mask based on clusters of the generator’s intermediate feature maps. A rearranging network then uses cross-attention to condition image generation on that proxy. The proxy provides an interface between the user’s semantic instructions and the internal features available in the pretrained generator.

The authors report that the semantic mapper and rearranging network can be trained in less than half an hour. Applications include mask-guided synthesis, spatial editing of real images, and local transplantation between unaligned images. Results span human faces, animal faces, and churches, demonstrating applicability across several kinds of imagery while reusing an unconditional generator.
neurips-2023-semantic-image-synthesis-wi.tldr: A semantic mapper and cross-attention rearranging network give pretrained unconditional generators detailed mask-based spatial control.

paragraphs: Federated bilevel optimization addresses nested learning problems distributed across clients, with applications including meta-learning, fine-tuning, and hyperparameter selection. Existing methods can require several inner loops during each iteration, with repeated communication inside those loops. This makes the optimization procedure complicated and communication-intensive even before accounting for differences among participating clients.

SimFBO removes these sub-loops and introduces generalized server-side aggregation and updating to improve communication efficiency. The authors also propose ShroFBO, a variant designed to better tolerate heterogeneous local computation. The two methods therefore address related practical concerns: simplifying the coordination procedure and making it more resilient when clients perform different amounts of computation.

The analysis establishes linear convergence speedup with partial client participation and sampling without replacement, along with improved sample and communication complexities. Experiments show effectiveness relative to existing federated bilevel algorithms. Together, these results connect a simpler algorithmic structure with theoretical efficiency gains and empirical improvements in the distributed nested-optimization setting studied by the paper.
neurips-2023-simfbo-towards-simple-flexi.tldr: SimFBO simplifies federated bilevel optimization by removing sub-loops, while ShroFBO adds resilience to heterogeneous client computation.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning data may come from environments whose dynamics differ, meaning the same action can have different consequences. Context-based methods often identify environment parameters and train corresponding policies, which can restrict how much data each policy uses. This paper seeks a reusable signal across environments with similar structures but different dynamics.

The authors observe that optimal policies in many such environments have similar stationary state distributions: their long-run patterns of state occupancy resemble one another. SRPO learns this distribution from data collected under differing dynamics and uses it to regularize a policy in a new environment. This allows data reuse through shared state-visitation patterns.

For theoretical analysis, the paper formalizes structural similarity through homomorphous Markov decision processes and establishes a lower-bound performance guarantee for distribution-regularized policies. SRPO can be added to context-based algorithms in both online and offline settings. Experiments show improved data efficiency and overall performance for several such algorithms, supporting reuse when the relevant environments share the state-distribution property motivating the method.
neurips-2023-state-regularized-policy-op.tldr: SRPO reuses data across differing dynamics by regularizing policies toward learned stationary state distributions shared by structurally similar environments.

paragraphs: Sampling from a distribution becomes more complicated when valid samples must satisfy geometric constraints. Barrier Hamiltonian Monte Carlo incorporates those constraints through a metric derived from a self-concordant barrier. This metric shapes the algorithm’s Hamiltonian dynamics, allowing its movement to reflect the geometry of the space on which the target Gibbs distribution is defined.

That geometric adaptation also creates a technical problem: the resulting differential equations are nonseparable, unlike the usual Euclidean case. The authors identify bias in existing manifold HMC generalizations arising in this setting. They introduce an additional filter, called an involution checking step, to address the problem and incorporate it into both continuous and numerical versions of the method.

The main results show that both versions generate Markov chains reversible with respect to the target distribution and avoid the bias identified in previous implementations. Numerical experiments use target distributions defined on polytopes. The contribution connects constraint-aware geometry with a correction that preserves the intended sampling distribution, rather than relying on geometric adaptation alone.
neurips-2023-unbiased-constrained-sampli.tldr: Barrier HMC combines constraint-aware geometry with an involution check that yields target-reversible sampling without the bias of previous implementations.

paragraphs: Face verification must decide whether two images show the same person, ideally using a single threshold to distinguish matching and nonmatching pairs. The paper argues that common training approaches do not fully address this requirement. Comparing samples with identity classes misses some relationships among individual images, while sample-to-sample training can require complicated pairing procedures.

The proposed unified threshold integrated sample-to-sample loss, or USS loss, explicitly includes a shared threshold for separating positive and negative pairs. The authors also derive sample-to-sample versions of softmax and binary cross-entropy losses and examine their relationships. This connects the verification decision rule more directly to the objective used during training.

USS can be combined with sample-to-class losses, and the resulting UniTSFace model uses it alongside a sample-to-class softmax loss. Evaluations across multiple benchmarks, including MFR, IJB-C, and MegaFace, report efficient operation and performance exceeding the compared state-of-the-art methods. The findings support combining pairwise relationships with class-based supervision while explicitly training for a unified verification threshold.
neurips-2023-unitsface-unified-threshold.tldr: UniTSFace combines a threshold-aware pairwise loss with class-based supervision to improve face recognition.

paragraphs: Knowledge tracing predicts students’ future performance from their earlier learning interactions. Many public datasets mainly describe those interactions through anonymous identifiers, even though educational context may help explain learning outcomes. XES3G5M adds richer information about questions and knowledge components, which represent concepts, principles, facts, or skills involved in solving them.

Collected from an online mathematics learning platform, the dataset contains 5,549,635 interactions from 18,066 students, covering 7,652 questions and 865 knowledge components. Its contextual information includes tree-structured relationships among knowledge components, question types, question text and analysis, and timestamps for student responses. These details allow models to use more than the identities of students and exercises.

The authors benchmark 19 state-of-the-art deep-learning knowledge-tracing models and find that using the auxiliary information is effective. The contribution therefore includes both a substantial dataset and an experimental basis for studying how educational context helps prediction. It broadens the available evidence for modeling learning processes beyond sequences composed primarily of anonymous problem and concept identifiers.
neurips-2023-xes3g5m-a-knowledge-tracing.tldr: XES3G5M provides millions of math-learning interactions with rich educational context and a benchmark showing the value of that information.
